Q: How can I debug my php cloud function in vscode A:

Try with these settings:

Edit your php.ini

zend_extension=xdebug

[xdebug]
xdebug.mode=debug
xdebug.start_with_request=yes
xdebug.client_host=127.0.0.1
xdebug.client_port=9003
xdebug.log_level=0

Restart your terminal after changes.

Create .vscode/launch.json.

{
  "version": "0.2.0",
  "configurations": [
    {
      "name": "Listen for Xdebug",
      "type": "php",
      "request": "launch",
      "port": 9003,
      "pathMappings": {
        "/workspace": "${workspaceFolder}"
      }
    }
  ]
}

Then test.

Q: MS Teams Bot to record meeting A:

This is a common sticking point with Teams. The officially supported path which comes with heavy constraints around permissions (needing to go through security reviews to get the host's tenant to approve permissions for most of the useful data).

If you are trying have a bot that joins using a meeting link like you mentioned you can either use the Teams Graph API and, accept the constraints around getting data, or you can do what most people do and avoid the native SDK route entirely and use a managed meeting bot that joins via the meeting link and captures audio and transcripts independently, rather than relying on the MS Teams Graph API.

Q: Conversion from HuggingFace dataset to Pandas DF causing dropped 'string' columns A:

By default, df.describe() does NOT show string columns. It only summarizes numeric columns. String (object) columns are not dropped — they are just not displayed.

You can check your code by this:

df.columns
df.dtypes
df.describe(include="all")

HuggingFace Dataset objects can have a format attached (e.g., torch, numpy). When a format is set, only the formatted columns are returned unless explicitly told otherwise.

To get consistent columns in both Huggingface and Pandas dataframe, you can use this code:

from datasets import load_dataset

pr_commits = load_dataset("hao-li/AIDev", "pr_commits")["train"]

pr_commits.reset_format()      # IMPORTANT
commits_df = pr_commits.to_pandas()

print(commits_df.columns)
print(commits_df.dtypes)

Hope it helps!

Q: How do type aliases (typing.Tuple, typing.Set, typing.List, etc.) work as an instance but also a class? A:

First of all, these aliases have been deprecated since 3.9. For 3.9+ code, just use tuple[...] instead of using typing.Tuple[...].

These aliases aren't types at runtime. They "work" because well-formed code won't use them in a way that needs them to be types, while static type checkers don't care about what happens at runtime.

>>> assert not isinstance(typing.Tuple, type)

They behave like instance objects since their constructors take arguments

They don't, actually. They don't even have constructors. The constructor to _SpecialGenericAlias takes arguments, as does the constructor to _BaseGenericAlias. But those aren't aliases themselves. They're superclasses of typing.Tuple, typing.List, and the other built-in aliases.

>>> typing.Tuple() # TypeError: Type Tuple cannot be instantiated; use tuple() instead

The pseudo-exception to this is parameterized user-defined generics, which are callable. Even then, however, Spam[object] isn't itself a type; it's an instance of typing._GenericAlias. Calling Spam[object](bar) just forwards the call to Spam.__init__ behind the scenes.

But they also behave like class objects: they satisfy isinstance() of a different class (for example (1,2,3) is a tuple but isinstance((1,2,3), Tuple) is also true

That's because _SpecialGenericAlias overrides __subclasscheck__:

class _SpecialGenericAlias(_NotIterable, _BaseGenericAlias, _root=True):
    ...
    def __subclasscheck__(self, cls):
        if isinstance(cls, _SpecialGenericAlias):
            return issubclass(cls.__origin__, self.__origin__)
        if not isinstance(cls, _GenericAlias):
            return issubclass(cls, self.__origin__)
        return super().__subclasscheck__(cls)
    ...

and _BaseGenericAlias overrides __instancecheck__ to use __subclasscheck__:

class _BaseGenericAlias(_Final, _root=True):
    ...
    def __instancecheck__(self, obj):
        return self.__subclasscheck__(type(obj))
    ...

This is basically just a hack; it changes the behavior of isinstance to use self.__origin__ (which represents the concrete type corresponding to the alias) instead of self (which is "supposed" to be a class but, for these aliases, isn't). Also, it only works on non-parameterized aliases. isinstance(object(), typing.Tuple[object] will throw an error.

Python type checkers (PyLance) accepts somevar : Tuple as a valid type

That's the whole point of the aliases. They don't do much at runtime; all of their power is in letting static type checkers pretend that they're types and handle static analysis accordingly.

Q: Missing symbol auto import functionality in Jupyter Notebook A:

Classic Jupyter Notebook doesn’t support IDE-style import resolution. Red squiggles/import this symbol type features come from language servers, and classic Jupyter has no LSP integration. To get similar behavior, you need to run notebooks in an environment that adds this layer. VS Code’s Jupyter notebooks work well and offer quick-fix auto-imports. JupyterLab can also do this with jupyterlab-lsp and a Python language server, though the results are less consistent. PyCharm and DataSpell work because they use a custom notebook editor rather than standard Jupyter.

Q: try catch block inside withTransaction breaks transaction A:

Yes, your observation is correct, and this behavior is expected with MongoDB transactions, even though it feels counter-intuitive at first.

The important thing to understand is:

  • Catching an error in your code does not mean the transaction is still valid.

When you use:

await session.withTransaction(async () => {
  // operations
});

the driver manages, retries and commit logic for you. Internally it:

  1. Starts a transaction
  2. Executes your callback
  3. Attempts to commit
  4. Retries the entire callback automatically if it sees certain retryable errors

However, some errors that occur during write operations automatically abort the transaction on the server, regardless of whether you catch them in JavaScript.

So, in this pattern:

try {
  await IOS_COL.insertOne(transaction, { session });
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err);
}

you are catching the exception at the application level, but MongoDB may already have marked the transaction as aborted.

Once that happens:

  • The transaction is no longer usable.
  • The next operation in the same transaction may fail with TransactionAborted or a TransientTransactionError.
  • The driver sees this label and retries the entire withTransaction() callback.
  • Your function runs again → same error → retry loop.

That explains why the callback appears to be called repeatedly.

Q: When exactly is the code verifier supposed to regenerated in PKCE flow? A:

You know, I think I figured out what the solution must be. The auth server gets rid of its challenge as soon as it does a verification step, right? That immediately renders any verifier useless until the next time the client sends it a new code challenge. That's why we don't need to generate a new challenge right away!
